US-CT.note: All public employees: state, municipal and teacher bargaining acts; the state code site (cga.ct.gov) was unreachable, so the fetched source shows the teacher statute only.

US-DC.note: All District government employees may bargain collectively under the Comprehensive Merit Personnel Act.

US-DE.note: State employees and local employers with 25+ full-time employees (or that opt in); teachers have a separate act (14 Del. C. ch. 40).

US-FL.cite: Fla. Const. art. I, § 6; Fla. Stat. § 447.301
US-FL.note: All public employees have a constitutional and statutory right to bargain collectively; recent laws added membership and recertification rules but kept the right.

US-GA.note: No general bargaining law; the teacher statute says nothing permits collective bargaining, and only firefighters have a local-option law (O.C.G.A. § 25-5-1 et seq.).

US-HI.note: All public employees: state and county employees and teachers bargain under HRS chapter 89, enforced by the Hawaii Labor Relations Board.

US-IA.note: All public employees keep the right, but since 2017 units with fewer than 30% public-safety members bargain only over base wages.

US-ID.note: Teachers (and firefighters under Idaho Code § 44-1801 et seq.) only; state and other local employees have no bargaining right.

US-IL.cite: 5 ILCS 315 (Illinois Public Labor Relations Act); 115 ILCS 5 (educational employees); Ill. Const. art. I, § 25
US-IL.note: All public employees: state and local workers under the Public Labor Relations Act and school employees under the Educational Labor Relations Act; a 2022 constitutional amendment added a right to bargain.

US-IN.note: Teachers only, limited to wages and benefits; state employees have had no bargaining since a 2005 executive order was rescinded, and other local employees have no statute.

US-KS.note: State employees and teachers are covered; other local employers come under the act only if their governing body elects it (the act says 'meet and confer').

US-KY.note: No general public-sector bargaining law; a public agency may choose to negotiate but has no duty to (Fayette County Educ. Ass'n v. Hardy, 1980); only some police and firefighter statutes exist.

US-LA.note: No public-sector bargaining statute; school boards and localities may bargain at their discretion (Louisiana Teachers' Ass'n v. Orleans Parish School Bd., 1974).

US-MA.note: All public employees: state, municipal and school employees bargain under chapter 150E.

US-MD.cite: Md. Code, State Pers. & Pens. § 3-501; Md. Code, Educ. §§ 6-402, 6-408
US-MD.note: State employees and public school employees bargain by statute; county and city employees depend on local law.

US-ME.note: All public employees: municipal, school, state and university employees bargain under separate acts.

US-MI.note: Local and school employees under PERA; classified state employees bargain under the Civil Service Commission's constitutional authority; the 2023 right-to-work repeal did not change this.

US-MN.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees bargain under the Public Employment Labor Relations Act.

US-MO.note: All public employees, including teachers and police, under the constitutional right to bargain as applied to the public sector in Independence-NEA v. Independence School District (2007); a 2018 restrictive law (HB 1413) was later struck down.

US-MS.note: No public-sector bargaining statute; teachers may join unions but employers have no duty to bargain (Jackson v. Hazlehurst Mun. Separate School Dist., 1983).

US-MT.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees.

US-NC.note: State law declares any public-sector collective bargaining contract illegal and void.

US-ND.note: Teachers only; state and other local employees have no bargaining right.

US-NE.note: All public employees, with disputes resolved by the Commission of Industrial Relations; state employees also under the State Employees Collective Bargaining Act.

US-NH.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees bargain under RSA 273-A.

US-NJ.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees.

US-NM.note: All public employees: state and local employees and teachers; the current act (2003) reinstated bargaining after the first act expired in 1999.

US-NV.note: Local government employees and teachers since 1969; state executive-branch employees were added by SB 135 (2019).

US-NY.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees under the Taylor Law.

US-OH.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees (the 2011 SB 5 limits were repealed by referendum).

US-OK.cite: 70 O.S. § 509.6 (teachers); 11 O.S. § 51-101 et seq. (police and fire)
US-OK.note: Teachers and police/fire only; state employees have no right, and the 2004 law for general employees of large cities was repealed in 2011.

US-OR.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees.

US-PA.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees under the Public Employe Relations Act; police and fire under Act 111.

US-RI.note: All public employees: state, municipal and school employees.

US-SC.note: Public employees have no right to collective bargaining (Branch v. City of Myrtle Beach, S.C. 2000), and no statute grants one.

US-SD.note: All public employees, including state employees, may designate representatives to meet and negotiate in good faith.

US-TN.note: No public-sector bargaining law; since 2011 teachers have only 'collaborative conferencing' on listed topics, which replaced bargaining.

US-TX.note: State law bars public employers from recognizing a union or signing a bargaining contract; only police and firefighters may bargain where local voters adopt it (Local Gov't Code ch. 143, 174).

US-UT.note: No statute gives public employees a bargaining right; HB 267 (2025) would ban it outright but was blocked on May 6, 2025 pending a November 3, 2026 referendum, and a reported December 2025 repeal was not verified here.

US-VA.note: No right: bargaining is barred unless a county, city, town or school board opts in by ordinance (allowed since May 1, 2021), and state employees are excluded.

US-VT.note: All public employees: state, municipal and school employees.

US-WA.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees.

US-WI.note: General municipal and school employees (and state employees) keep a right to bargain limited to total base wages since Act 10; a Dane County ruling of 12/2/2024 struck much of Act 10 but was on appeal, and either way a bargaining right existed on 1/1/2026.

US-WV.note: No public-sector bargaining statute; employers may negotiate voluntarily but no binding bargaining right exists.

US-WY.note: Only firefighters have a bargaining statute (Wyo. Stat. § 27-10-101 et seq.); school boards may bargain voluntarily (1978 Att'y Gen. opinion).

us-policy-positions:fiscal.balanced-oper.source: NASBO Budget Processes in the States (2021 edition, Table 9 and notes; the current edition linked from nasbo.org as of 9/28/2026) for the 50 states and D.C.; NASBO Budget Processes in the Territories (2024, Table 5) for Guam, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands; primary constitution and code pages fetched for CA, ID, MN, OH, VA, WA and D.C. No state law change between 2021 and 1/1/2026 that removes a requirement was found.
us-policy-positions:fiscal.balanced-oper.note: Unknown, and left out: US-AS, US-MP.

US-AK.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory). NASBO cites AS 37.07.020(c) (governor) and AS 37.07.014(e)(2) (legislature).

US-AL.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional and statutory).

US-AR.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-AZ.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory). Arizona may carry a General Fund deficit; there is no rule to cure it next cycle.

US-CA.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional). Since fiscal 2004-05 the legislature may not send, nor the governor sign, a General Fund budget exceeding estimated revenue. The governor-submit, pass and sign requirements are constitutional.

US-CO.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-CT.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory).

US-DC.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional). The Home Rule Act requires the mayor's budget to be prepared so that expenditures do not exceed resources.

US-DE.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-FL.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-GA.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional).

US-GU.note: Per NASBO's 2024 territories survey (Table 5), the governor must submit, the legislature must pass and the governor must sign a balanced budget in Guam; Guam has no year-end rule and reports occasional operating deficits.

US-HI.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory). NASBO calls the requirement implied by the constitution and statute; a year may end in deficit if prior balances cover it.

US-IA.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-ID.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-IL.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory).

US-IN.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: legislature must pass one (constitutional). This is the weakest form: Indiana may carry annual deficits and relies mainly on the constitutional debt ban.

US-KS.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-KY.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-LA.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-MA.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-MD.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional). The governor does not sign the budget bill; the enacted budget must be balanced.

US-ME.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional and statutory).

US-MI.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-MN.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional and statutory). NASBO says the constitutional debt limit implies balance and cites Minn. Stat. 16A.11, subd. 2.

US-MO.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-MS.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-MT.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-NC.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional and statutory).

US-ND.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-NE.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory). NASBO marks a constitutional carryover rule but no year-end check; the biennium must balance and a first-year deficit is allowed.

US-NH.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory). The biennium must balance, but it may use prior-biennium fund balances.

US-NJ.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-NM.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-NV.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (statutory).

US-NY.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (statutory); budget signed must be balanced (basis not specified); no deficit carryover at year-end (basis not specified).

US-OH.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional and statutory). The constitution caps debt for casual deficits at $750,000 (art. VIII, sec. 1).

US-OK.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-OR.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-PA.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory).

US-PR.note: Per NASBO's 2024 territories survey (Table 5), the governor must submit, the legislature must pass and the governor must sign a balanced budget in Puerto Rico; it may not carry a deficit over.

US-RI.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional). The rule is derived from the constitutional cap on borrowing without voter approval; a deficit may be carried into the next year.

US-SC.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional and statutory).

US-SD.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-TN.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-TX.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-UT.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional).

US-VA.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional). The requirement applies only to budget execution: the governor must keep expenses within revenue over the biennium (Va. Const. art. X, sec. 7).

US-VI.note: Per NASBO's 2024 territories survey (Table 5), the governor must submit, the legislature must pass and the governor must sign a balanced budget in U.S. Virgin Islands; it may not carry a deficit over.

US-VT.note: Vermont is the only state reporting no constitutional or statutory balanced budget requirement, though NASBO notes it has never carried a deficit over in practice.

US-WA.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (statutory); legislature must pass one (statutory). RCW 43.88.055 also requires a four-year balanced budget from the 2013-15 biennium.

US-WI.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional and statutory); legislature must pass one (constitutional and statutory); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional and statutory). The deficit must be corrected in the next fiscal year.

US-WV.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional and statutory). NASBO does not mark a governor-submit requirement for West Virginia.

US-WY.note: Per NASBO 2021 Table 9: governor must submit a balanced budget (constitutional); legislature must pass one (constitutional); budget signed must be balanced (constitutional); no deficit carryover at year-end (constitutional and statutory).

us-policy-positions:fiscal.exempt-grocer.source: State code and revenue pages fetched 9/28/2026 (AL, ID, IL, KS, MS, MO, OK, SD, TN, UT, VA and 16 state codes plus D.C.); Tax Foundation 'The Surprising Regressivity of Grocery Tax Exemptions' (updated 9/13/2023), '2026 State Tax Changes' and '2026 Sales Tax Rates Midyear'; Wikipedia 'Sales taxes in the United States' table as a cross-check.
us-policy-positions:fiscal.exempt-grocer.note: Unknown, and left out: US-AS, US-GU, US-MP, US-PR, US-VI.

US-AK.note: No state sales tax; some Alaska boroughs and cities levy local sales taxes, and many of those apply to groceries.

US-AL.note: Alabama taxes groceries at a reduced state rate of 2% (4% general rate), plus local taxes; the rate was cut from 4% in steps starting in 2023, and the exact date of the step to 2% was not confirmed on a fetched page.

US-AR.note: Arkansas repealed its 0.125% state sales tax on groceries effective January 1, 2026 (HB1685, the Grocery Tax Relief Act); local sales taxes still apply to groceries.

US-AZ.note: Some Arizona cities tax food under their own transaction privilege taxes.

US-CO.note: Colorado exempts food for home consumption from the state tax; many home-rule cities and some counties tax groceries. State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-CT.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-DC.note: D.C. excludes SNAP-eligible food from taxable retail sales.

US-DE.note: No state sales tax.

US-FL.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-GA.note: Georgia exempts groceries from the 4% state tax; local sales taxes of up to 4% apply to groceries. State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-HI.note: Hawaii's 4% general excise tax (plus any county surcharge) applies to groceries at the full rate; there is a refundable food/excise tax credit for lower-income residents.

US-IA.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-ID.note: Idaho taxes groceries at the full 6% state rate and offsets it with an income tax grocery credit of $155 per person from tax year 2025.

US-IL.note: Illinois eliminated its 1% state grocery tax on January 1, 2026; counties and municipalities may impose a 1% local grocery tax by ordinance, and many did.

US-IN.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-KS.note: Kansas cut its state rate on food and food ingredients to 0% on January 1, 2025 (from 4% in 2023 and 2% in 2024); local sales taxes still apply.

US-KY.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-LA.note: Louisiana exempts food for home consumption from the state tax; local parish and city taxes apply. State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-MO.note: Missouri taxes food for home consumption at a reduced state rate of 1.225% (general rate 4.225%), plus full local rates.

US-MS.note: Mississippi taxes groceries (SNAP-eligible food) at a reduced state rate of 5% against a 7% general rate; the cut from 7% to 5% took effect July 1, 2025 (date per the Mississippi DOR notice cited in Wikipedia; the fetched rates page shows only the current 5%).

US-MT.note: No state sales tax.

US-NC.note: Food is exempt from the state tax; a 2% local tax applies to groceries.

US-ND.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-NH.note: No state sales tax.

US-NJ.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-NM.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-NY.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-OK.note: Oklahoma exempted food and food ingredients from the 4.5% state sales tax on August 29, 2024 (HB 1955); city and county sales taxes still apply.

US-OR.note: No state sales tax.

US-PA.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-RI.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-SC.note: The exemption covers the state tax only; local sales taxes can apply to groceries.

US-SD.note: South Dakota taxes groceries at the full 4.2% state rate; voters rejected a grocery exemption (Initiated Measure 28) in November 2024.

US-TN.note: Tennessee taxes food at a reduced state rate of 4% (general rate 7%), plus local taxes.

US-TX.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

US-UT.note: Utah taxes food at a reduced state rate of 1.75% plus local rates (about 3% combined), against a general state rate of 4.85%.

US-VA.note: Virginia removed the state portion of its grocery tax on January 1, 2023, but the 1% local sales tax still applies to groceries throughout the state.

US-WV.note: West Virginia's tax on food and food ingredients ceased after June 30, 2013.

US-WY.note: State exemption confirmed by a Tax Foundation list of states that tax groceries (updated 9/13/2023; this state is not on it), matched by the 2026 Wikipedia sales-tax table; no later change found.

us-policy-positions:fiscal.fund-pensions.source: State code pages fetched 9/28/2026 (AK, AZ, CA, CO, DC, DE, IA, ID, KS, KY, MA, MD, MI, MN, MO, NC, ND, NE, NV, OH, OR, PA, RI, SD, VA, VT, WA, WI, WY); TRS Illinois 2025 valuation; NASRA 'ARC Experience of State Retirement Plans' (March 2015), 'State Legal Provisions Addressing Pension Funding' (April 2017), and 'Employer Contributions' issue brief (January 2026) for the rest.
us-policy-positions:fiscal.fund-pensions.note: Unknown, and left out: US-AS, US-GU, US-MP, US-MS, US-PR, US-VI.

US-AK.note: Employers pay 22 percent of pay and the state must pay the rest of the board-adopted actuarial rate for the closed PERS plan each year.

US-AL.note: State law requires employers in the Retirement Systems of Alabama to pay the actuarially determined contribution (NASRA 2015 summary; no later change found).

US-AR.note: APERS and ATRS employers must pay the actuarially determined contribution by statute, though the teachers' employer rate is capped (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-AZ.note: Employer contributions to the Arizona State Retirement System must equal normal cost plus the amount to amortize the unfunded liability, as set by the board's actuary.

US-CA.note: The Legislature must adopt the CalPERS board's actuarial contribution rates and appropriate them in the Budget Act; CalSTRS state contributions follow a separate statutory funding plan.

US-CO.note: PERA employer rates are fixed percentages of pay in statute, with a small automatic increase (up to 0.5 percent a year, capped at 2 points) only when total contributions fall below 98 percent of the actuarial requirement.

US-CT.note: State statutes require the actuarially determined contribution for SERS and the Teachers' Retirement Board (NASRA 2015 summary; the state statute site could not be fetched).

US-DC.note: The Retirement Board certifies the actuarially determined District payment each year, and the Mayor and Council must budget no less than that amount.

US-DE.note: The state's appropriation must equal the board-approved actuarial rate: normal cost plus 20-year amortization of the unfunded liability.

US-FL.note: The Legislature sets Florida Retirement System employer rates in statute each year after an actuarial study; no law forces it to adopt the full actuarial rate (NASRA 2015 summary; the Florida statute site was not reachable).

US-GA.note: Georgia statutes require ERS and TRS employers to pay the actuarially determined contribution, and the state constitution requires actuarial funding standards (NASRA 2015 and 2017 summaries).

US-HI.note: Hawaii ERS employer contributions are fixed percentages of pay set in statute, not the actuarial amount (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-IA.note: IPERS contributions are the actuarially determined rate, split 60/40 employer/employee for regular members, but the regular rate may not change more than one percentage point a year.

US-ID.note: PERSI employers must pay normal cost plus an amortization payment at rates the board sets from the actuarial valuation.

US-IL.note: State contributions follow a statutory ramp toward 90 percent funding by 2045, which is well below the actuarially determined contribution (TRS 2025 valuation).

US-IN.note: State statute directs the board to calculate, and the legislature to fund, the actuarially determined contribution (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-KS.note: KPERS certifies an actuarial employer rate each year, but statute caps each year's increase (now 1.2 percent of pay), and lawmakers set fixed rates in several recent years.

US-KY.note: KERS and State Police employers must pay the actuarial normal cost plus the unfunded liability payment each year; the teachers' system uses fixed employer rates, and the state must make up any shortfall in the next budget.

US-LA.note: The state constitution requires the legislature to fund the employer normal cost each year and amortize the unfunded liability on a set schedule.

US-MA.note: The state pays a statutory funding schedule (for example, $4.93 billion in FY2026) designed to pay off the unfunded liability, not the annually determined actuarial contribution; the schedule's growth is also capped.

US-MD.note: The state must pay at least the actuarial normal rate plus accrued liability rate for each state system; 2013 legislation ended the older below-actuarial corridor method.

US-ME.note: The state constitution requires normal cost to be funded each year on an actuarially sound basis and experience losses to be paid off within 10 years.

US-MI.note: School retirement contribution rates must be set by annual actuarial valuation, including a payment on the unfunded liability.

US-MN.note: Minnesota employer contributions are fixed percentages of salary set in statute.

US-MO.note: The MOSERS board certifies the actuarial rate and the commissioner must request that appropriation; NASRA reads this as a statutory actuarial requirement, but the teachers' plan uses a statutory rate.

US-MT.note: Montana PERS and TRS employer contributions are fixed percentages of pay set in statute (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-NC.note: The yearly payment to the pension fund may not be less than the actuarially determined employer contribution rate.

US-ND.note: State agencies must pay normal cost plus the actuarially determined amount to amortize the main PERS plan over a closed period beginning 1/1/2026, or the legislature may transfer at least that amount; the teachers' fund still uses fixed rates.

US-NE.note: For the school plan, the state must pay any gap between the statutory rates and the actuarially required rate; the state and county cash balance plans also require the actuarial contribution.

US-NH.note: The state constitution requires the actuarially certified employer contributions to be appropriated each fiscal year.

US-NJ.note: Statute calls for the actuarial contribution, but courts ruled it does not bind future legislatures; the state has paid the full amount since FY2022 as a budget choice, and a 2016 constitutional amendment failed to reach the ballot.

US-NM.note: New Mexico PERA and ERB employer contributions are fixed percentages of pay set in statute (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-NV.note: Nevada PERS contribution rates are the actuarially determined rates from the biennial valuation.

US-NY.note: State law requires employers in the NY State and Local Retirement System and NYSTRS to pay the actuarially determined contribution (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-OH.note: Employer rates are calculated actuarially, but statute caps the OPERS employer rate at 14 percent of pay, so the full actuarial amount is not required.

US-OK.note: Oklahoma PERS and TRS employer contributions are fixed percentages of pay in statute, plus dedicated tax revenue for TRS (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-OR.note: Employers must pay what the PERS board determines is actuarially necessary to fund benefits.

US-PA.note: PSERS employers pay the actuarially required rate, except that a rate collar limits how much it can rise in one year.

US-RI.note: The state must appropriate each year the actuarially computed percentage covering normal cost and the amortization of the unfunded liability.

US-SC.note: The state constitution requires yearly appropriations sufficient on a sound actuarial basis, as determined by the system's governing body.

US-SD.note: Employers match member contributions at fixed statutory rates (6 percent for Class A); the system instead must propose benefit changes when those rates fall short.

US-TN.note: Employers in the Tennessee Consolidated Retirement System must pay the actuarially determined contribution by statute (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-TX.note: The constitution limits the state's contribution to ERS and TRS to 6 to 10 percent of pay outside emergencies, and statutes set fixed rates; ERS also has statutory legacy payments.

US-UT.note: Utah statutes require Utah Retirement Systems employers to pay the actuarially determined contribution (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-VA.note: Employer contribution rates must be the actuarial normal plus accrued liability rates set biennially by the VRS board.

US-VT.note: The state must pay the actuarially determined employer contribution, plus extra fixed amounts while the fund is below 90 percent funded.

US-WA.note: The Pension Funding Council adopts actuarial rates, but the legislature may revise them, and statute sets some plan 1 rates to zero through 6/30/2029.

US-WI.note: Contributions are set at the total actuarially required contribution rate approved by the board and split between employer and employee.

US-WV.note: PERS employers pay board-set rates meant to fund the actuarial contribution, and the state must pay extra to amortize the Teachers' system on a statutory schedule (NASRA 2015 summary).

US-WY.note: The employer rate is fixed at 9.37 percent of pay through 6/30/2026; starting with the 2027-2028 biennium (7/1/2026), rates must be based on the actuarially determined contribution.

us-policy-positions:fiscal.cap-property-.source: Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, Significant Features of the Property Tax, assessment-limit and levy-limit summary tables (2022 data, published 12/2024 and 1/2025); state constitutions and codes fetched 9/28/2026 (CA, AZ, DC, FL, MD, MI, NV, OR, SC, TX, WY, IA, MO, SD); Georgia DOR bulletin 2025-01; Cook County Assessor.
us-policy-positions:fiscal.cap-property-.note: Unknown, and left out: US-AS, US-GU, US-MP, US-PR, US-VI.

US-AK.note: No per-property cap; municipalities face levy caps only.

US-AL.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found in the Lincoln Institute 2022 table; post-2022 enactments not separately verified.

US-AR.note: Assessment cap: after a countywide reappraisal, a homestead's assessed value may rise no more than 5% a year and other real property no more than 10% a year (Lincoln Institute 2022 table; primary text not fetched).

US-AZ.note: Assessment cap: the taxable (limited) value of all real property may rise no more than 5% a year over the prior year's limited value, for all property taxes since tax year 2015.

US-CA.note: Assessment cap (Proposition 13): the assessed value of all real property may rise no more than 2% a year, or inflation if lower, until the property sells or is newly built.

US-CO.note: No per-property cap; Gallagher was repealed in 2020 and the 2024 laws limit local property tax revenue growth (a levy limit) and cut assessment rates.

US-CT.note: No per-property cap; towns may only choose to phase in a revaluation increase over up to five years.

US-DC.note: Assessment cap by credit: an owner-occupied homestead is taxed on no more than 110% of last year's taxable assessment (102% for seniors and disabled owners); the excess is credited on the bill.

US-DE.note: No per-property cap; county levies are rolled back after reassessment.

US-FL.note: Assessment cap (Save Our Homes): a homestead's assessed value may rise no more than 3% a year or inflation if lower; other property is capped at 10% a year for non-school taxes.

US-GA.note: Assessment cap: a statewide floating homestead exemption holds a homestead's taxable assessed value to its base-year value adjusted for inflation (frozen for 2025, CPI from 2026), but each county, city or school district could opt out, and many school systems did.

US-HI.note: No state-law cap; counties hold property tax power under the state constitution, and any caps are county ordinances (not verified).

US-IA.note: No per-property cap; Iowa's 3% limit applies to aggregate statewide residential and agricultural value through a rollback, so an individual home can rise more.

US-ID.note: No per-property cap; local levy growth is capped at 3% a year.

US-IL.note: No general per-property cap; the old Cook County 7% homestead cap has ended, and what remains in Cook County (7% or 10% a year) is limited to long-time owners with household income of $100,000 or less, plus an income-limited senior freeze; PTELL is a levy limit.

US-IN.note: No growth cap; the circuit-breaker caps a bill at 1% of gross assessed value for homesteads (a rate cap, not a growth cap), plus levy limits.

US-KS.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found; post-2022 enactments not separately verified.

US-KY.note: No per-property cap; local levies are limited by revenue-growth rules.

US-LA.note: No percentage cap; a homestead reappraisal increase of more than 50% is phased in over four years, and millages roll back after reassessment.

US-MA.note: No per-property cap; Proposition 2 1/2 limits each community's levy growth to 2.5% a year.

US-MD.note: Assessment cap by credit: a homestead's taxable assessment for state tax may rise no more than 10% a year, and each county or city sets its own cap between 0% and 10%.

US-ME.note: No per-property cap; municipalities face a levy limit (LD 1).

US-MI.note: Assessment cap (Proposal A): each parcel's taxable value may rise no more than 5% a year or inflation if lower, until ownership transfers.

US-MN.note: No per-property cap; the old limited-market-value phase-in ended, and levy limits apply.

US-MO.note: No per-property cap; an assessor must physically inspect before raising a home's value more than 15%, and counties may adopt an optional senior freeze.

US-MS.note: No per-property cap; local levies are capped.

US-MT.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found in the Lincoln Institute 2022 table.

US-NC.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found in the Lincoln Institute 2022 table.

US-ND.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found in the Lincoln Institute 2022 table; later levy limits do not cap individual bills.

US-NE.note: No per-property cap; local levies are capped.

US-NH.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found in the Lincoln Institute 2022 table.

US-NJ.note: No per-property cap; the 2% cap limits local levies.

US-NM.note: Assessment cap: residential property's taxable value may rise no more than 3% a year (or 6.1% over two years), reset on sale (Lincoln Institute 2022 table; primary text not fetched).

US-NV.note: Tax-bill cap: an owner-occupied single-family home's property tax bill may rise no more than 3% a year through a partial abatement; other property has a separate, higher abatement cap.

US-NY.note: Assessment cap only in New York City and Nassau County: one-to-three-family homes may rise no more than 6% a year and 20% over five years; the statewide 2% cap limits local levies, not individual bills.

US-OH.note: No per-property cap; tax reduction factors roll back voted levies after reappraisal.

US-OK.note: Assessment cap: taxable value may rise no more than 3% a year for homesteads and farm land and 5% for other property (Lincoln Institute 2022 table; the state court site that hosts the constitution blocked automated fetches).

US-OR.note: Assessment cap (Measure 50): each property's maximum assessed value may rise no more than 3% a year, and a sale does not reset it.

US-PA.note: No per-property cap; levies are rolled back after countywide reassessment.

US-RI.note: No per-property cap; municipal levies are capped at 4% growth a year.

US-SC.note: Assessment cap: at each five-year countywide reappraisal a property's value may rise no more than 15% (about 2.8% a year), reset on sale or new improvements.

US-SD.note: No per-property cap; a new 3% limit (SDCL 10-6-158, 2025) applies to each county's total owner-occupied assessed value, not individual homes, and starts with taxes payable in 2027.

US-TN.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found in the Lincoln Institute 2022 table.

US-TX.note: Assessment cap: a homestead's appraised value may rise no more than 10% a year; a temporary 20% cap on non-homestead property valued up to about $5 million runs through 2026.

US-UT.note: No per-property cap; truth-in-taxation rules roll back the certified rate as values rise.

US-VA.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found in the Lincoln Institute 2022 table.

US-VT.note: No per-property assessment or bill growth cap found in the Lincoln Institute 2022 table.

US-WA.note: No per-property cap; each taxing district's levy may grow only 1% a year.

US-WI.note: No per-property cap; local levies are limited.

US-WV.note: No per-property cap; levies are rolled back after reappraisal.

US-WY.note: Assessment cap by exemption: any rise in a single-family home's (and its lot's) assessed value above 4% a year is exempt, reset on sale or structural additions.

us-policy-positions:fiscal.minimum-reser.source: Statute and constitution pages fetched on 9/28/2026 for 31 states and D.C.; the NASBO 'Budget Processes in the States' 2021 Tables 13 and 15 for the rest; the NASBO 'Budget Processes in the Territories' report (2023–24) for Guam.
us-policy-positions:fiscal.minimum-reser.note: Unknown, and left out: US-AS, US-KY, US-MP, US-NJ, US-NM, US-PR, US-VI.

US-AK.note: Oil and gas tax settlement money must go into the Constitutional Budget Reserve, and year-end surpluses are swept into it; the deposit is not a fixed share of spending (NASBO 2021).

US-AL.cite: Ala. Const. amend. 803; Education Trust Fund Budget Stabilization Fund statute
US-AL.note: Up to 1% of the prior year's Education Trust Fund appropriations must move from the fund's ending balance into its Budget Stabilization Fund each year until that fund reaches 7.5% of appropriations (NASBO 2021).

US-AR.note: By statute, the Long Term Reserve Fund must be replenished by a transfer from the General Revenue Allotment Reserve Fund (50% of its balance or the prior year's draws, whichever is less) (NASBO 2021).

US-AZ.note: When revenue grows faster than trend, a formula sets the deposit (excess growth times general fund revenue) the legislature is to appropriate to the Budget Stabilization Fund, up to a cap tied to revenue.

US-CA.note: The Controller must transfer 1.5% of estimated General Fund revenue each year, plus a share of excess capital-gains revenue, into the Budget Stabilization Account until it reaches 10% of General Fund tax revenue.

US-CO.note: Statute requires a General Fund reserve equal to a set percentage of appropriations that must be refilled if it is spent (7.25% in NASBO 2021; the percentage has since been changed by statute).

US-CT.note: Unappropriated surplus and revenue from volatile taxes, chiefly capital gains, must be deposited into the Budget Reserve Fund until it reaches 15% of General Fund appropriations (NASBO 2021).

US-DC.note: The Mayor must keep the emergency cash reserve at 2% of operating expenditures (§ 1-204.50a), and year-end fund balance must fill the Fiscal Stabilization Reserve (2.34% of expenditures) and the Cash Flow Reserve (10% of the operating budget).

US-DE.note: Under the constitution, the excess of unencumbered funds at year end must be paid into the Budget Reserve Account until it reaches 5% of estimated General Fund revenue (NASBO 2021).

US-FL.note: At least 5% of the last completed fiscal year's general revenue collections must be kept in the Budget Stabilization Fund, and the fund may not exceed 10%.

US-GA.note: By statute, General Fund money left over after the year's spending lapses into the Revenue Shortfall Reserve, which is capped at 15% of prior-year net revenue (NASBO 2021).

US-GU.note: Deposits into the Rainy Day Fund are set as a percentage of projected general fund revenue, and the fund must hold at least 2% of projected revenue (NASBO territories report, 2023–24).

US-HI.note: The Emergency and Budget Reserve Fund must receive 5% of the general fund balance when conditions in the constitution and HRS § 328L-3 are met (NASBO 2021).

US-IA.note: The year-end General Fund surplus must go to the Cash Reserve Fund, and a further transfer of up to 1% of revenue is made when needed to reach the 7.5% goal; any excess then goes to the Economic Emergency Fund, capped at 2.5%.

US-ID.note: When general fund receipts grow more than 4%, the controller must transfer the excess, up to 1% of the prior year's collections, to the Budget Stabilization Fund, which is capped at 10% of receipts.

US-IL.note: A 2004 statute directs surplus revenue to the Budget Stabilization Fund and Pension Stabilization Fund, but NASBO reports that no such transfer has ever occurred; other deposits are by appropriation.

US-IN.note: By statute, General Fund money moves into and out of the Economic Stabilization Fund automatically according to the annual growth rate of adjusted personal income (NASBO 2021).

US-KS.note: By statute, the enacted budget must leave an unspent State General Fund balance of 7.5% of expenditures, and the Budget Stabilization Fund receives a share of revenue above the consensus estimate (NASBO 2021).

US-LA.note: Mineral revenue above $950 million and 25% of nonrecurring revenue must go into the Budget Stabilization Fund until it reaches 4% of total state revenue receipts (NASBO 2021).

US-MA.note: Available consolidated net surplus must be transferred to the Commonwealth Stabilization Fund, along with excess capital gains, within a cap tied to revenue.

US-MD.note: The Governor must budget $100 million, or $50 million, for the Revenue Stabilization Account whenever its balance is below 7.5% of revenue, and nonwithholding income tax above the cap must be deposited; fiscal year 2026 is exempt from the minimum appropriation.

US-ME.note: The Budget Stabilization Fund may not fall below 1% or exceed 18% of the prior year's General Fund revenue, and it receives a set share of the year-end unappropriated surplus.

US-MI.note: A formula sets a pay-in when personal income grows more than 2%, but the legislature must provide every transfer into the fund through an appropriations act, and NASBO calls the formula advisory.

US-MN.note: A forecast general fund balance must first fill the $350 million cash flow account and then the budget reserve up to its statutory target.

US-MO.note: The Budget Reserve Fund must hold 7.5% of the previous year's net general revenue collections (NASBO 2021).

US-MS.note: Statute fixes the order in which the General Fund's year-end unencumbered cash is distributed, including to the Working Cash Stabilization Reserve Fund, which is capped at 10% of appropriations (NASBO 2021).

US-MT.note: Each August, unspent general fund appropriations above 0.5% of the year's total must be transferred to the Budget Stabilization Reserve Fund, except in years with required budget cuts.

US-NC.note: Each budget act must transfer 15% of estimated General Fund tax revenue growth to the Savings Reserve, or the smaller amount needed to reach its recommended balance.

US-ND.note: At the end of each biennium, general fund money above $65 million must be transferred to the Budget Stabilization Fund, which is capped at 15% of appropriations.

US-NE.note: General Fund net receipts above the certified forecast must be transferred to the Cash Reserve Fund.

US-NH.note: Unless another law provides otherwise, any audited biennial general fund surplus must be transferred to the Revenue Stabilization Reserve Account.

US-NV.note: Each year the Controller must transfer 1% of anticipated revenue, plus 40% of the year-end General Fund balance above 7% of appropriations, to the Account to Stabilize the Operation of State Government.

US-NY.note: A year-end general fund cash surplus, up to 0.2% of the year's disbursements, must be transferred to the Tax Stabilization Reserve Fund until that fund reaches 2%.

US-OH.note: Each July, surplus revenue must be transferred to the Budget Stabilization Fund until it equals 10% of the prior year's general revenue fund revenue.

US-OK.note: Revenue collected above 100% of the estimate must go into the Constitutional Reserve Fund until it reaches 15% of the prior year's General Revenue collections (NASBO 2021).

US-OR.note: After each biennium, 1% of General Fund appropriations (or the whole ending balance, if smaller) must be transferred to the Rainy Day Fund; the Education Stability Fund also receives a constitutional share of lottery proceeds.

US-PA.note: By statute, 25% of the General Fund's year-end surplus must be transferred to the Budget Stabilization Reserve Fund, falling to 10% once the fund reaches 6% of revenue (NASBO 2021).

US-RI.cite: R.I. Const. art. IX, § 17; R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 35-3-20, 35-3-20.1
US-RI.note: Spending is limited to 97% of revenue, and 3% of general revenue must be set aside in the Budget Reserve and Cash Stabilization Account, which is capped at 5%.

US-SC.note: The General Reserve must equal 5% of the most recently completed year's general fund revenue, and a Capital Reserve of 2% must also be kept (NASBO 2021).

US-SD.note: All prior-year unobligated cash must be transferred to the budget reserve fund until it reaches 10% of the prior year's general fund appropriations.

US-TN.note: By statute, 10% of state tax revenue growth allocated to the General and Education Funds must be set aside in the Reserve for Revenue Fluctuations, which is capped at 8% (NASBO 2021).

US-TX.note: Half of any unencumbered general revenue balance at the end of each biennium must be transferred to the Economic Stabilization Fund, which also receives oil and gas tax revenue, within a cap (NASBO 2021).

US-UT.note: The Division of Finance must transfer 25% of any General Fund revenue surplus to the General Fund Budget Reserve Account until the account reaches its cap (8% of appropriations in NASBO 2021; the version effective 5/6/2026 says 9%).

US-VA.note: When income and sales tax revenue grows faster than its six-year average, the General Assembly must deposit at least half of the above-trend growth into the Revenue Stabilization Fund, which is capped at 15% of average revenue.

US-VT.note: Any undesignated General Fund surplus at year end must be reserved in the Budget Stabilization Reserve up to 5% of the prior year's appropriations.

US-WA.note: By June 30 of each fiscal year, the treasurer must transfer 1% of general state revenue to the Budget Stabilization Account.

US-WI.note: When tax collections exceed the budget projection, the secretary must transfer 50% of the difference to the Budget Stabilization Fund.

US-WV.note: Up to the first 50% of each year's surplus revenue must be deposited into the Revenue Shortfall Reserve Fund; since 7/1/2024 the target is 20% of a three-year average of appropriations (it was 13% earlier).

US-WY.note: The Governor must recommend a General Fund reserve of at least 5% of estimated receipts, and any unappropriated General Fund balance above that reserve at the end of each biennium must be transferred to the Legislative Stabilization Reserve Account.

US-AZ.note: At least two-thirds of any government body that investigates officer misconduct or recommends or imposes discipline must be certified officers from the officer's own department, so a civilian board may only review decisions after the fact.

US-CA.note: Counties may create civilian sheriff oversight boards and an inspector general with subpoena power over the sheriff's department; AB 1185 took effect in 2021 and AB 847 (ch. 383) amended the section effective 1/1/2026.

US-DC.note: The District's Office of Police Complaints and Police Complaints Board receive, investigate and adjudicate civilian complaints against Metropolitan Police officers.

US-FL.cite: Fla. Stat. § 112.533(3) (ch. 2024-86, Laws of Fla., HB 601)
US-FL.note: Since 7/1/2024 local governments may not adopt ordinances on investigating police misconduct complaints or on civilian oversight of those investigations; sheriffs and police chiefs may set up civilian boards that only review policies.

US-MA.note: The Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission, a nine-member board with a civilian majority, has a division of police standards that receives every agency's complaints, investigates officer misconduct and recommends discipline up to decertification.

US-MD.cite: Md. Code, Pub. Safety §§ 3-102, 3-104 (Police Accountability Act of 2021)
US-MD.note: Every county must have a police accountability board that takes public complaints and an administrative charging committee with civilian members that reviews each misconduct investigation, can require more investigation and subpoenas, and decides whether to charge the officer.

US-MN.note: Local governments may create civilian oversight councils that investigate misconduct after any criminal case, subpoena testimony and documents, and make findings and recommend discipline to the chief.

US-MO.note: Since 2000 cities and counties may create civilian review boards to receive, investigate and make findings on public complaints; a 2024 amendment (SB 754, effective 8/28/2024) limits them to those powers and voids any broader authority.

US-NV.note: Cities and counties may create civilian review boards whose panels review internal investigations, recommend discipline and may subpoena witnesses and documents; they have no jurisdiction over alleged crimes.

US-TN.cite: Tenn. Code Ann. Title 38, Ch. 8 (Pub. Ch. 454, 2023, SB 591)
US-TN.note: The 2023 law abolished community oversight boards and lets cities create police advisory and review committees that send complaints to internal affairs, review its files and may only ask for further investigation; they have no subpoena power.

US-VA.note: Localities may create civilian oversight bodies that investigate complaints, issue findings, make binding discipline decisions in serious cases and seek court subpoenas (2020 Special Session I, cc. 29-30).

US-WA.note: The 2021 law created the Office of Independent Investigations in the governor's office to investigate police uses of deadly force independently of police agencies; it covers serious incidents, not every complaint.

US-WI.note: State law gives each city's citizen police and fire commission the power to hear charges filed by any aggrieved person against an officer and to impose discipline; it is a hearing board rather than an investigating office.

US-AK.note: Home-rule boroughs and cities may exercise all legislative powers not prohibited by law or charter, and the constitution orders liberal construction of every local government's powers.

US-AL.note: Cities and towns hold only the powers the legislature delegates to them, and counties have no general grant at all, so Dillon's Rule governs.

US-AR.note: Act 1187 of 2011 gave every municipality full legislative power over municipal affairs and declared Dillon's Rule inapplicable; before that, only first-class cities had it. Section 14-43-601 lists the matters reserved as state affairs.

US-AZ.note: Only charter cities (population over 3,500, including Phoenix and Tucson) hold home rule, and their charters prevail over conflicting laws on city matters; the general-law cities, which are most cities by count, have only statutory powers.

US-CA.note: Every county and city may make any local police, sanitary and other regulations that do not conflict with general laws, and charter cities also control their municipal affairs.

US-CO.note: The 103 home-rule municipalities, including Denver, may legislate on local matters, but statutory towns remain strictly subject to state law.

US-CT.note: The General Assembly delegates only the legislative authority it chooses to towns, cities and boroughs, and the Home Rule Act lets them choose their charter structure but not residual powers. The source is a Wikisource copy because cga.ct.gov refused connections.

US-DC.note: The District has no municipalities, and its own legislative power extends to all rightful subjects of legislation, subject to the Home Rule Act's limits and Congress's reserved power to legislate for the District at any time.

US-DE.note: A municipality with at least 1,000 residents that amends its charter under this chapter gains every power the General Assembly could grant and that no statute denies; smaller towns and those that have not amended keep only their charter powers.

US-FL.cite: Fla. Const. art. VIII, § 2(b); Fla. Stat. § 166.021
US-FL.note: All municipalities may exercise any power for municipal purposes except when expressly prohibited by law, and the statute removes judicially imposed limits.

US-GA.cite: Ga. Const. art. IX, § II, ¶ II; O.C.G.A. § 36-35-3
US-GA.note: By statute, cities may adopt reasonable ordinances on their affairs where general law makes no provision and that are consistent with the constitution; counties hold home rule directly under the constitution.

US-HI.note: Hawaii has no incorporated cities, and its counties exercise only the powers conferred under general laws; their charters control structure and organization, not residual lawmaking power.

US-IA.cite: Iowa Code § 364.1; Iowa Const. art. III, § 38A
US-IA.note: Every city may exercise any power it deems appropriate unless expressly limited by the constitution or inconsistent with state law.

US-ID.note: Every city may exercise all powers of local self-government in city affairs that are not specifically prohibited by or in conflict with state law.

US-IL.note: Home-rule municipalities (automatically those over 25,000 residents, others by referendum) may exercise any power not specifically prohibited by state law, while non-home-rule municipalities have only granted powers.

US-IN.note: Indiana's counties, cities and towns are exempt from Dillon's Rule, which applies there only to townships. The source is only the Wikipedia table's comment, because the Indiana Code site returned only a script shell.

US-KS.note: All cities may determine their local affairs and government, subject to uniform state laws, and their powers are construed to give them the largest measure of self-government. The source is a Wikisource copy because state hosts refused.

US-KY.note: Every city may exercise any power in furtherance of a public purpose that does not conflict with the constitution or a statute.

US-LA.note: Home-rule-charter governments may exercise any power not denied by general law, and a noncharter government gains the same power if its voters approve; otherwise it has only the powers the law grants.

US-MA.note: Every city and town may exercise any power the General Court could confer that is not inconsistent with its laws and not denied by the local charter.

US-MD.cite: Md. Const. art. XI-E; Md. Code, Local Gov't § 5-202
US-MD.note: Municipalities hold constitutional home rule and a general grant to adopt ordinances for good government, public safety, health and welfare; this is a general-welfare grant rather than an express 'any power not denied' clause.

US-ME.note: Every municipality may exercise any power the Legislature could confer that is not denied expressly or by clear implication.

US-MI.cite: Mich. Comp. Laws § 117.4j(3); Mich. Const. art. 7, § 22
US-MI.note: Home-rule cities (all Michigan cities) may exercise all municipal powers, whether or not enumerated, subject to the constitution and general law; townships remain under Dillon's Rule.

US-MN.cite: Minn. Stat. § 410.07; Minn. Const. art. XII, § 4
US-MN.note: Home-rule charter cities, which include Minneapolis and Saint Paul, may regulate all local municipal functions as fully as the legislature could; statutory cities, which are most cities by count, hold only granted powers.

US-MO.note: Charter cities hold every power the General Assembly could confer unless the charter or a statute limits or denies it; noncharter cities have only statutory powers.

US-MP.cite: N. Mar. I. Const. art. VI, § 7(a)
US-MP.note: Municipal councils' powers extend to all matters of a predominantly local nature not preempted by the Commonwealth Legislature, but their listed powers are budget and confirmation duties. The source is a Wikisource copy that could not be checked against cnmilaw.org, which returned only a script shell.

US-MT.note: Only local governments that adopt a self-government charter may exercise any power not prohibited; general-power governments have narrower powers.

US-NC.note: City powers must still come from a grant; the statute only requires broad construction of granted powers and their reasonably necessary supplements.

US-ND.note: Home-rule cities hold self-government only 'within the powers enumerated' in the statute's list, and only as their charters include them.

US-NE.note: Only cities over 5,000 may frame a home-rule charter, and only Lincoln and Omaha have one; the constitutional text is a charter grant 'subject to the constitution and laws', and every other city lives under Dillon's Rule.

US-NH.note: Towns may adopt bylaws only on the subjects the statute lists, so Dillon's Rule governs.

US-NJ.note: The constitution orders liberal construction of municipal and county powers in their favor, including implied and incidental powers, and New Jersey is usually classed as a home-rule state; the general police-power statute could not be fetched.

US-NM.note: New Mexico's home-rule municipalities hold broad powers, while the others keep only granted powers. The only source available is Wikipedia's table, because nmonesource.com and the Secretary of State's copy of the constitution could not be fetched.

US-NV.note: Nevada keeps Dillon's Rule, modified since 2015 to give city governing bodies implied power over matters of local concern; those matters exclude statewide interests. The brief's definition classes this as Dillon's Rule; see conflicts.

US-NY.note: Every local government may adopt local laws relating to its property, affairs or government that are consistent with the constitution and general law. The source is a Wikisource copy as of 2004; this clause has been unchanged since 1963.

US-OH.note: All municipalities hold all powers of local self-government and may adopt local police regulations that do not conflict with general laws.

US-OK.note: Cities over 2,000 may frame their own charter; the text is a charter grant 'consistent with and subject to' state law, and its broader scope comes from court doctrine on municipal affairs. Noncharter towns have only statutory powers.

US-OR.note: The voters of every city and town may enact and amend their own municipal charter, subject to the constitution and criminal laws.

US-PA.note: Only municipalities that adopt a home-rule charter may exercise any power not denied by the constitution, the charter or the General Assembly; most of Pennsylvania's municipalities have not adopted one.

US-PR.cite: Código Municipal de Puerto Rico (Ley 107-2020), arts. 1.007, 1.008, 1.010
US-PR.note: Municipalities may order, regulate and resolve whatever is necessary or convenient for local needs, and their listed powers are non-exclusive and construed liberally; the autonomy they exercise is conferred by the Legislative Assembly. See conflicts.

US-RI.note: Every city and town has self-government in all local matters and may enact local laws on its property, affairs and government consistent with state law.

US-SC.note: Every municipality may legislate on any subject it finds necessary and proper for its security, general welfare and good government, consistent with the constitution and general law.

US-SD.note: Only a chartered (home-rule) county or city may exercise any legislative power not denied by its charter, the constitution or general law; few municipalities have adopted a charter.

US-TN.note: Tennessee home rule means only that the 14 home-rule cities control their own charters and are shielded from private acts; it does not grant residual powers, and most cities hold only statutory powers.

US-TX.note: Home-rule municipalities (cities over 5,000 that adopt a charter) have full power of local self-government; general-law cities have only granted powers.

US-UT.note: Municipalities have a broad general-welfare power to pass ordinances for the safety, health, prosperity and order of their residents, and the Utah Supreme Court rejected Dillon's Rule in State v. Hutchison (1980).

US-VA.note: Virginia is a Dillon's Rule state: a locality may act only where the General Assembly has clearly granted authority. See conflicts about Va. Code § 15.2-1102.

US-VT.note: Towns, cities and villages hold the powers the statute enumerates, plus their charter powers, so Dillon's Rule governs.

US-WA.note: Code cities, the majority of Washington cities, hold all powers possible for a city under the constitution that no law specifically denies, and every city holds the local police power under Wash. Const. art. XI, § 11.

US-WI.note: Cities and villages may determine their local affairs and government, subject only to the constitution and uniform statewide legislation.

US-WV.note: City powers are enumerated but construed without strict construction, and the Municipal Home Rule Program lets only approved cities carry out their board-approved written plans.

US-WY.note: All cities and towns may determine their local affairs by ordinance, subject only to statutes that apply uniformly to all cities and towns; taxes require legislative authorization.
